While such actions may seem unreasonable to those of a more traditional mindset. In many ways, this is a positive development. In the first instance, many health care systems are currently overburdened with very long waiting times to see medical professionals. By switching to alternatives, potential patients are no longer becoming so and helping to alleviate the pressure on the healthcare infrastructure. Of course, this could increase medical issues if the alternative treatments make conditions worse or delay vital support. However, many homeopathic medicines can produce psychosomatic or placebo effect, which can address some conditions as effectively as such. As effectively as standard medical treatment. While this raises certain ethical concerns, the benefits to beleaguered health services are clear. Additionally, in countries with socialized medicine where public funding support standard healthcare providers, a lower number of patients waiting for or receiving treatment should reduce the amount of money spent on this, leaving more available to fund those who use the service. Assuming medical goods and services are taxed appropriately, for example, through VAT, then the money which is spent on this could be used to fund traditional services. Alternatively, the taxes from this could be used to monitor public health to ensure any issues being obscured by the rise in alternative medicine use are noticed before they become serious. To conclude, not only is the increasing uptake in alternative medicine, addressing the issue of waiting times to see a medical professional, it can also save the taxpayer money in countries with welfare states.
